traditionalCourse: Adult Health / Med-Surg II & Critical Care
title: Major Burns & Inhalation Injury: Airway, Resuscitation and Recovery
html:
A burn can threaten the airway, breathing, circulation, limb perfusion, temperature control, kidney function, infection resistance, mobility, nutrition, body image, and mental health. The visible wound is only one part of the injury. The RN stops ongoing exposure, applies trauma priorities, estimates depth and total body surface area (TBSA), detects inhalation or hidden electrical and chemical injury, supports response-guided resuscitation, and begins function-preserving care immediately.

Learning goals

  • Prioritize airway, ventilation, perfusion, trauma, and hypothermia prevention during initial burn care.
  • Differentiate burn depth from TBSA and apply adult Rule of Nines, palmar method, and referral criteria safely.
  • Recognize upper-airway edema, lower-airway injury, carbon monoxide exposure, and possible cyanide toxicity.
  • Explain why the current adult burn-resuscitation formula is only a starting estimate and requires hourly titration.
  • Identify limb- or ventilation-threatening circumferential burns and hidden chemical or electrical injury.
  • Integrate wound, tetanus, pain, infection, nutrition, mobility, scar, and psychosocial care.

Stop burning, then prevent hypothermia

Ensure scene safety and stop the burning process. Remove the patient from the source; remove hot or contaminated clothing and jewelry unless adhered; brush away dry chemical before irrigation when appropriate; and disconnect electrical power before touching the person. For a small thermal injury, cool running water—not ice—can limit ongoing heat injury. Do not apply ice, butter, oils, toothpaste, or unapproved ointments. Avoid prolonged cooling of a large burn because hypothermia worsens coagulopathy and outcomes.

Cover the patient with a clean, dry sheet or dressing and maintain a warm environment. Apply the trauma primary survey: protect the cervical spine when mechanism warrants, assess airway and breathing, control major hemorrhage, evaluate circulation and disability, then expose enough to find all injuries while preventing heat loss. A burn does not protect against fractures, internal bleeding, traumatic brain injury, or spinal injury.

Depth and TBSA answer different questions

Superficial burns are dry, red, blanching, and usually painful; they are not included in burn-resuscitation TBSA. Superficial partial-thickness burns are commonly moist, red, blanching, blistered, and very painful. Deep partial-thickness burns may be drier, pale or mottled, less blanching, and less painful as nerve endings are damaged. Full-thickness burns can be white, brown, black, dry, or leathery with reduced pinprick sensation. Mixed depth is common, and wounds can evolve during the first days.

TBSA estimates the area of partial- and full-thickness injury. In adults, the Rule of Nines assigns the head and neck 9%, each arm 9%, each leg 18%, anterior trunk 18%, posterior trunk 18%, and perineum 1%. For small scattered burns, the patient's entire palmar surface is approximately 1%, but the team must use one consistent definition. Children require an age-adjusted Lund–Browder chart because body proportions differ. Reassess the estimate after cleansing and burn-specialist review.

The American Burn Association recommends immediate burn-center consultation with consideration for transfer for full-thickness burns; partial-thickness burns at least 10% TBSA; deep partial- or full-thickness burns of the face, hands, genitalia, feet, perineum, or over joints; suspected inhalation injury; high-voltage electrical or lightning injury; chemical injury; significant comorbidity or associated trauma; or poorly controlled pain. Smaller or potentially deep burns may still warrant consultation. Follow regional capability and transfer agreements.

Airway injury can worsen after arrival

Suspect inhalation injury after an enclosed-space fire, smoke exposure, facial or neck burn, singed facial hair, soot in the mouth or sputum, carbonaceous secretions, hoarseness, cough, wheeze, stridor, respiratory distress, altered mentation, or progressive swelling. Absence of an external facial burn does not exclude injury. Upper-airway edema can progress rapidly after fluids begin, making later intubation difficult.

Give high-concentration humidified oxygen for suspected smoke inhalation and summon airway expertise early. Prepare for early endotracheal intubation when airway patency, gas exchange, ventilation, mental status, secretion clearance, or safe transport is threatened. Stridor is a late warning, not a finding to await. Do not perform prophylactic intubation from singed nasal hair alone; integrate mechanism, symptoms, examination, trajectory, transport time, and specialist input.

Carbon monoxide binds hemoglobin and impairs oxygen delivery. Standard pulse oximetry can appear normal because it cannot reliably distinguish oxyhemoglobin from carboxyhemoglobin. Obtain co-oximetry when available, but do not delay 100% oxygen for a symptomatic smoke-exposed patient. Headache, dizziness, nausea, confusion, syncope, ischemia, or severe exposure increases concern. Possible cyanide toxicity in a closed-space fire may produce severe lactic acidosis, hypotension, cardiovascular collapse, or altered consciousness; antidote decisions require an emergency or toxicology pathway.

Burn shock formulas only start the conversation

Large burns increase capillary permeability, cause intravascular volume loss and edema, and can produce burn shock. The 2023 American Burn Association guideline addresses adults with burns at least 20% TBSA and recommends initiating crystalloid resuscitation from 2 mL × body weight in kilograms × percent TBSA for the first 24 hours to reduce excessive volume. This is a starting estimate—not a fixed prescription or proof that every patient needs the calculated total.

Time begins at the moment of injury, not hospital arrival. A protocol commonly provides approximately half of the estimated first-day amount during the first eight hours from injury and the remainder over the next 16 hours, then titrates hourly to response and burn-center guidance. Include prehospital fluid in the total. Do not count superficial erythema in TBSA or use a child formula for an adult. Children, electrical injuries, delayed presentation, pregnancy, heart or kidney disease, and associated trauma require individualized protocols.

For most adults, hourly urine output near 0.5 mL/kg/hour is a common resuscitation target, interpreted with MAP, heart rate, mentation, capillary refill, lactate or base deficit trend, respiratory status, edema, and laboratory findings. A formula error should be corrected early, but oliguria is not an automatic command to keep increasing fluid. Check catheter patency, perfusion, abdominal pressure, kidney injury, rhabdomyolysis, and other causes.

Fluid creep—progressive administration beyond physiologic need—can worsen pulmonary edema, extremity or abdominal compartment syndrome, orbital pressure, tissue edema, and graft outcomes. Record the exact hourly input, urine output, weight, hemodynamics, airway pressures, limb findings, and cumulative balance. Escalate a rising fluid requirement or poor response instead of silently increasing rates. Selected patients need intra-abdominal or intraocular-pressure monitoring; albumin and other adjuncts belong to a burn-center plan.

Circumferential burns threaten perfusion and ventilation

Rigid full-thickness eschar around an extremity can restrict circulation as edema develops. Compare pulses and Doppler signals, capillary refill, color, temperature, pain, sensation, movement, swelling, and compartment tension at frequent intervals. A palpable pulse does not exclude evolving ischemia. Remove constricting items, elevate as directed, mark Doppler sites, and immediately report worsening pain, paresthesia, weakness, coolness, delayed refill, or loss of signal.

A circumferential chest or abdominal burn can restrict expansion and raise airway pressures. Increasing work of breathing, reduced chest excursion, rising ventilator pressures, or worsening ventilation requires immediate burn and surgical assessment. Escharotomy releases burned tissue; fasciotomy addresses deeper muscle-compartment pressure. Neither is a routine bedside nursing intervention, and improvement requires repeated neurovascular or ventilatory reassessment.

Chemical and electrical burns hide ongoing injury

For chemical exposure, protect staff with appropriate PPE, remove contaminated clothing, and identify the substance if possible. Brush off dry powder before irrigation when the product requires it, then use copious water irrigation for most skin exposures. Eye exposure requires immediate continuous irrigation and ocular pH or specialist-directed assessment. Do not blindly neutralize an acid with an alkali or the reverse because the reaction may generate heat. Some agents require substance-specific management; consult poison control, hazardous-material, and burn resources.

Electrical injury can produce deep muscle, nerve, vascular, and organ damage despite small entry and exit wounds. Confirm that power is off, assess for falls or blast trauma, obtain cardiac and neurovascular assessment, and monitor for dysrhythmia according to voltage, symptoms, ECG, and protocol. Dark urine, muscle pain or swelling, hyperkalemia, rising creatine kinase, acidosis, or kidney injury suggests rhabdomyolysis. Escalating pain, tense compartments, sensory or motor change, or diminished perfusion can signal compartment syndrome. High-voltage and lightning injuries require burn-center consultation.

Wound care, pain, infection and nutrition

Clean and cover burns according to the burn-team plan. Maintain aseptic technique, describe depth, color, moisture, tissue, drainage, odor after cleansing, surrounding erythema, and changes, and never apply a constrictive dressing. Topical products, debridement, blister management, biologic dressings, excision, and grafting depend on depth, location, contamination, healing trajectory, allergy, and specialist direction. Routine systemic antibiotics do not prevent burn-wound infection and can promote resistance; treat a suspected or confirmed infection using cultures and the current plan.

Burns contain devitalized tissue and are considered dirty or major wounds for tetanus decisions. Review the primary series and last tetanus-containing vaccine. Vaccination and tetanus immune globulin depend on wound category, vaccine history, HIV or severe immunodeficiency, and current CDC guidance. Antibiotics are not a substitute for tetanus prophylaxis.

Assess background and procedural pain separately from anxiety, itch, and neuropathic symptoms. Premedicate before dressing care and therapy, combine opioid and nonopioid strategies when safe, monitor sedation and breathing, and use nonpharmacologic support. Less pain in a pale or leathery wound may mean deeper nerve destruction—not improvement.

Major burns create a hypermetabolic, catabolic state. Support early enteral nutrition when ordered, adequate protein and energy, glucose monitoring, micronutrient and electrolyte assessment, bowel function, and daily weight interpreted with fluid balance. Avoid relying on albumin alone as a nutrition marker during acute inflammation.

Rehabilitation starts on day one

Edema, pain, immobilization, graft precautions, and scar contraction can rapidly reduce function. Coordinate positioning, elevation, splinting, active or passive range of motion, mobility, respiratory hygiene, and activities of daily living with burn, physical, occupational, respiratory, and surgical teams. Protect grafts and donor sites while avoiding unnecessary prolonged immobility. A wound closing is not the same as recovery.

Screen for sleep disturbance, delirium, acute stress, depression, anxiety, post-traumatic stress, substance concerns, body-image distress, caregiver needs, work and housing barriers, and nonaccidental injury. Use trauma-informed communication and include the patient in dressing, pain, rehabilitation, and discharge decisions. Teach wound and graft care, infection cues, moisturization after closure, sun protection, scar care, exercise, nutrition, and follow-up.

Apply clinical judgment

  1. Recognize cues: Identify mechanism, time, enclosed-space or chemical exposure, trauma, airway and breathing change, depth, TBSA, critical locations, neurovascular status, temperature, urine output, and comorbidities.
  2. Analyze cues: Connect airway trajectory with edema, interpret pulse oximetry limits in carbon monoxide exposure, separate depth from area, and compare inadequate perfusion with harmful over-resuscitation.
  3. Prioritize hypotheses: Threatened airway, toxic inhalation, hypoxemia, shock, major associated trauma, compartment syndrome, circumferential chest restriction, severe chemical eye injury, and electrical dysrhythmia require immediate action.
  4. Generate solutions: Stop exposure, warm and oxygenate, obtain expert airway and burn consultation, estimate injury accurately, start authorized response-guided fluid, protect perfusion, and prepare source-specific treatment.
  5. Take action: Remove constriction, administer prescribed oxygen, analgesia and fluids, monitor hourly response, protect wounds aseptically, update tetanus prophylaxis, and preserve motion and dignity.
  6. Evaluate outcomes: Reassess airway, gas exchange, hemodynamics, mentation, temperature, urine output, neurovascular findings, edema, wound progression, pain, nutrition, mobility, infection, and coping.

Clinical example

An adult rescued from an enclosed house fire has a 25% partial- and full-thickness burn, hoarse voice, soot in the mouth, headache, and a pulse oximeter reading of 99%. The RN does not interpret the displayed saturation as reassurance. The RN applies 100% oxygen, calls for early airway and burn-center evaluation, prepares co-oximetry and other ordered toxic-exposure studies, estimates TBSA without counting superficial erythema, begins protocol-directed crystalloid from the injury time, inserts a urinary catheter when ordered, and trends perfusion and respiratory status. Increasing hoarseness or work of breathing prompts airway control before edema makes intubation more difficult.

Original educational synthesis. Airway management, toxic-exposure treatment, burn-depth and TBSA estimation, transfer, fluid calculation and titration, escharotomy or fasciotomy, chemical decontamination, electrical monitoring, wound products, antimicrobial therapy, tetanus prophylaxis, graft care, nutrition, and rehabilitation require current patient data, authorized orders, product information, local protocols, poison-control resources, and burn-specialist direction. This lesson is not medical advice, clinical decision support, continuing education, certification, or an official ABA or CDC product.
